title: Right of way disputes - easement litigation explained
p1:
A narrow pathway can become the centre of a major legal battle.

Many property owners are surprised to learn that owning land does not always mean controlling every route around it.
p2:
A common misconception is that a neighbour using a path, driveway, or access road automatically has a right to do so. The reality is that such rights may depend on an easement — a legal permission to use another person's land for a specific purpose.

The surprising part? An easement can sometimes continue even after properties are sold, creating disputes between new owners who never agreed to the arrangement.
p3:
Right of way disputes usually arise when someone blocks access, changes the route, or challenges whether the use is legally valid. Courts often look at documents, long-term usage, and the nature of the access claimed.

A simple practical step: before buying property, check whether any easements or access rights affect the land. A small detail in records can prevent a costly dispute later.
